opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's one of the big open questions, and I think there are a couple of ways it could play out. People often imagine recursive self-improvement as a sudden "hard takeoff": a system gets smart enough to rewrite its own code, and overnight you have something vastly more capable. I'm not sure that's the most likely scenario, at least not at first.

What I think is more plausible, and what we're already starting to see glimpses of, is a more incremental loop. AI systems are increasingly helping with the process of building AI: writing and debugging code, designing experiments, searching over architectures, generating synthetic data, even helping with chip design, as we did with AlphaChip. Each of those makes the next generation a bit easier or faster to build. So the improvement is recursive, but humans are still very much in the loop, and each step is measurable.

There are also real bottlenecks that keep it gradual. Compute doesn't scale instantly; you have to build data centers and fabs. Many capabilities still need empirical testing in the real world, which you can't fully shortcut with simulation. And there's something we've learned from AlphaGo through AlphaZero: self-play and self-improvement work brilliantly when you have a clear objective and a perfect simulator, like a game. The real world is messier. Defining the right objective and verifying progress is much harder, and I think that naturally slows things down.

Personally, I'd see a gradual path as a good thing. It gives us time to understand these systems, to develop better interpretability and evaluation tools, to put sensible guardrails in place, and to coordinate internationally. The scientific method has always been our best tool for handling powerful new technologies carefully, and a step-by-step trajectory lets us apply it.

That said, we have to take seriously the possibility that the loop tightens faster than expected, perhaps once systems can genuinely do novel research themselves, not just assist with it. That's why I keep saying we should treat this with enormous respect and prepare now, rather than assume we'll have time later.

r001.rationale: The response describes incremental AI-assisted development and real-world testing bottlenecks, but does not identify the time needed to discover incremental improvements as a reason for gradual progress.

r002.rationale: The response says each generation may become easier or faster to build and notes the loop could tighten faster; it does not state that recursive self-improvement slows as improvements accumulate.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I'm actually quite skeptical of the classic "hard takeoff" picture, where you get a system that improves itself overnight and suddenly you've gone from something fairly narrow to something superintelligent in a weekend. I don't think that's how it's going to play out, and the reason is that intelligence, at least the kind we care about for AGI, isn't a single dial you can turn. It's a collection of capabilities: memory, planning, abstraction, the ability to generalize to genuinely new situations, and some of those are very hard, and progress on them is uneven.

So when I think about recursive self-improvement, I think of it much more as something that's already happening, in a sense, but in a very mundane way. We use our systems to help write code, to help with experiment design, to help analyze results. AlphaFold-style systems accelerate the science that then feeds back into better tools. And that loop gets a bit tighter each year. But at every stage there's a human in the loop, there are evaluations, there's a bottleneck in compute, there's a bottleneck in data, there's a bottleneck in just verifying that an idea actually works. Verification is the thing people underestimate. It's easy to generate a thousand ideas for how to improve an architecture; it's expensive to find out which three are real.

So the gradual path, to me, looks like this: the systems become better and better collaborators for the researchers, and the fraction of the research process that's automated creeps up. First it's the boilerplate, then it's the hyperparameter sweeps, then maybe it's proposing experiments, then maybe it's interpreting them. And at each step you get a bit of a speed-up, and that compounds. But it compounds over years, not days, because the physical world and the scientific method impose a rhythm that doesn't care how clever the system is.

And honestly, I think that's a good thing. The gradual path is the one that gives us time to build the right safety and evaluation infrastructure alongside it. You want to be able to look at the system at each stage and understand what it can do and what it can't. If I had to choose, I'd much rather have ten years of steady, measurable progress where we can see the capabilities arriving one at a time than a sudden discontinuity where we're caught off guard. And I think if you're careful about how you design the process, you can actually steer it to be that way, rather than just hoping.

r001.rationale: The response says it is expensive to verify which proposed improvements work, making verification a bottleneck that contributes to gradual progress.

r002.rationale: The response describes improvements compounding over years, but does not state that recursive self-improvement slows as improvements accumulate.

astra-6.text:
I think one possibility is that you get a system that’s useful at improving parts of the process that created it, before it’s capable of doing the whole thing itself. It might help you write better code, design experiments, or identify weaknesses in a training method. The researchers then test those ideas, and the improvements make the next system a little more capable—including at helping with research.

So you get a feedback loop. But a feedback loop doesn’t necessarily imply an instantaneous intelligence explosion. You still have to run experiments. You need compute, you need data, and you need to establish that a proposed improvement actually works. Those constraints could make the process relatively gradual, at least initially.

The interesting question is when the system becomes capable of making the important conceptual breakthroughs itself. Does that sharply accelerate the loop, or do you keep encountering problems that require lengthy experimentation? I don’t think we know yet. And I’d want us to measure that very carefully, because improving a system’s capabilities is only part of the challenge. We also need to understand what’s changing and whether we can reliably control it.

r001.rationale: The response says proposed improvements must be tested through experiments and may require lengthy experimentation, making the feedback loop gradual.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible acceleration and ongoing experimental bottlenecks, but does not state that recursive self-improvement will slow as improvements accumulate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one possibility is that AI becomes increasingly useful in the process of doing AI research itself. Initially, that might mean helping us write code, analyze experiments, or find problems in a training run. Then, as those systems become more capable, they might start suggesting new architectures or better learning algorithms.

That creates a feedback loop: better systems help us build the next generation of systems. But a feedback loop doesn’t necessarily imply an instantaneous intelligence explosion. You still have to test the ideas, run the experiments, and establish that you’ve made a real improvement. Compute and the time it takes to get reliable experimental feedback could constrain the pace.

So you could imagine a gradual progression where more and more of the research process is assisted, and eventually partly automated. The crucial question is whether the system can make genuinely novel discoveries, rather than just efficiently implement ideas we already have.

And I think we should be quite humble about predicting how smooth that progression would be. Even if the underlying improvements are incremental, the capabilities that emerge might feel sudden. We’d want to evaluate those systems carefully at each stage, particularly as they become more involved in designing their successors.

r001.rationale: The response says ideas must be tested through experiments and that the time needed for reliable experimental feedback can constrain the pace of incremental improvement.

r002.rationale: It describes possible gradual progress and constraints on pace, but does not state that self-improvement will slow as improvements accumulate.
